A.taste_why: The panel is restrained: one PanelSectionHeader "WINDOW OPACITY", then two labelled rows with a muted percentage beside each. It uses the bar foreground and font and the 󰗋 icon with a "Window opacity" tooltip, adding nothing unrequested. Nothing is applied until a slider is first moved, so Hyprland's own config stays in charge, which is a thoughtful default. The plain Text labels with a "› " bold selection marker look a little less native than the CursorSurface outline used by the others.
A.implementation_why: It uses `hyprctl -q eval` with an hl.config Lua call through a single Process. Drags coalesce through `pending` and `onExited: flush()`. A configreloaded handler with an echoGuard timer re-applies saved values without looping. Settings are clamped and validated and persisted through updateEntryInline. The code is compact and readable. Weaknesses: `nudge` calls save() on every keypress with no debounce, so shell.json is written each time, and `dragging` is a manual flag rather than the slider's own state.
A.execution_why: It has a bar button that opens a small panel with Focused and Unfocused sliders. Opacity changes live through hyprctl eval. Settings are saved in shell.json and re-applied on shell start and after Hyprland reloads, so they survive a restart. It does everything asked and nothing more.

B.taste_why: It uses the native PanelHero and CursorSurface, so it looks at home. It adds a Reset button and a "100% = OMARCHY DEFAULT" meta line, and scrolling on the bar icon silently changes the focused-window opacity. That wheel behaviour is an unrequested and surprising extra. The 30% floor is sensible.
B.implementation_why: Coalescing is solid (applyQueued plus onRunningChanged), persistence is debounced, and the reload guard is time-based. Weaknesses: the apply path runs `bash -c` with an eval-then-`hyprctl keyword` fallback, which is needless machinery. Component.onCompleted applies 100/100 even when nothing has been saved, so it overrides the user's Hyprland config on every start. The 1500ms timestamp guard is cruder than checking actual state.
B.execution_why: It meets every part of the request: bar button, a panel with two live sliders, and values persisted in shell.json and re-applied after restart and reload. It loses a little for the unrequested wheel-scroll adjustment and the Reset button.

C.taste_why: The panel is clean: icon and title row, separator, FOCUSED/UNFOCUSED section headers with percentages, and CursorSurface outlines. The tooltip shows both current percentages, which is useful. Before anything is saved the sliders mirror Hyprland's live values, which is a sensible default. It adds no gimmicks. The header is hand-built from Text items rather than PanelHero, which is minor.
C.implementation_why: Reconciliation is careful: it reads `hyprctl -j getoption`, adopts the live values until something is saved, and re-applies only when Hyprland disagrees, so reloads never loop. Persistence is debounced and flushed when the panel closes. Weaknesses: execDetached on a 30ms timer can spawn many hyprctl processes during a drag. The default-property-alias slider plumbing is somewhat more machinery than needed.
C.execution_why: Everything requested is present. Both sliders change opacity live through hyprctl eval. Values are saved in shell.json and re-enforced on load and after configreloaded, so they survive restarts.

D.taste_why: The UI is native-looking: a hero with icon and title, a subtitle "APPLIED LIVE · SAVED", and CursorSurface rows. It also adds wheel-on-icon adjustment, which was not asked for, and the subtitle is mildly misleading since the values are not actually kept.
D.implementation_why: The header comment says ~/.config/hypr/window-opacity.lua reads the state file, but no such file is shipped or written. It saves to $XDG_STATE_HOME through a `bash -c` mkdir/printf/mv pipeline instead of the shell's settings API. The read path runs bash, hyprctl and jq. It uses `hyprctl keyword` where the others use the Lua eval API. The saved file is consulted only when hyprctl fails to answer.
D.execution_why: The live sliders work. Persistence is effectively broken: after a restart, refresh() reads Hyprland's current config values first and never re-applies the saved file. The "keep my settings after a restart" requirement therefore fails.

verdict.ranking_why: A and C both fully deliver live sliders and shell.json persistence with reload re-apply. A is leaner and more restrained. C adds smarter reconciliation but spawns many hyprctl processes during drags. B works but adds unrequested wheel scrolling and a Reset button, and forces 100% on every start. D's persistence depends on a Lua file it never creates, so settings do not survive a restart.
